lesson.title: Meet the Family: Parent Functions
lesson.summary: A parent function is the simplest, unmodified equation in a family of related graphs, serving as the reference point for every transformation.
lesson.body:
A parent function is the simplest, most stripped-down equation that represents an entire family of related functions. Every quadratic function, no matter how it has been shifted, stretched, or flipped, shares the same basic U-shape as the parent quadratic f(x) = x^2, and every absolute value function shares the same V-shape as the parent function f(x) = |x| from the last chapter. Learning the parent function first gives you a stable reference point, a known shape and set of key values, that every other member of the family can be compared against.

Algebra 1 introduces a handful of core parent functions: the linear parent f(x) = x, a straight line through the origin with slope 1; the quadratic parent f(x) = x^2, a U-shaped curve called a parabola; the absolute value parent f(x) = |x|, the V-shape from the previous chapter; the cubic parent f(x) = x^3, an S-shaped curve; and the square root parent f(x) = sqrt(x), which only exists for x >= 0. Each of these has its own signature shape, and each one is the plainest, least-modified version of its family, with no shifting, stretching, or flipping applied yet.

Consider the parent quadratic f(x) = x^2 and build a table of values around x = 0. At x = -2, f(-2) = (-2)^2 = 4. At x = -1, f(-1) = 1. At x = 0, f(0) = 0. At x = 1, f(1) = 1. At x = 2, f(2) = 4. Plotting these five points, (-2, 4), (-1, 1), (0, 0), (1, 1), and (2, 4), shows a symmetric U-shape with its lowest point, the vertex, sitting at the origin, and the graph is a mirror image of itself across the y-axis.

Now compare that to a close relative, g(x) = x^2 + 3. Using the same inputs, g(-2) = 4 + 3 = 7, g(-1) = 1 + 3 = 4, g(0) = 0 + 3 = 3, g(1) = 4, and g(2) = 7. Every single output is exactly 3 more than the corresponding output of the parent function, which means the entire graph has simply been slid upward by 3 units, keeping the exact same U-shape and width. Nothing about the curve's shape changed, only its position.

The linear parent f(x) = x and the cubic parent f(x) = x^3 both pass through the origin and increase from lower left to upper right, but the cubic flattens out near the origin and rises much more steeply farther away: f(2) = 2 for the line, but f(2) = 8 for the cubic. The square root parent f(x) = sqrt(x) looks different from all the others because its domain stops at x = 0, since negative numbers have no real square root; f(4) = 2 and f(9) = 3, and the graph only exists to the right of the y-axis, curving upward more and more slowly as x grows.

That sliding behavior, where a small change to the equation moves or reshapes the parent graph in a predictable way without changing its fundamental character, is called a function transformation, and it is powerful precisely because it lets you understand an entire family of complicated-looking equations just by remembering one simple parent and a short list of rules for how it moves. That short list of rules is the subject of the next chapter.
